newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian budget could widen scope of expenditure tax.
newsitem.headline: Indian budget could widen scope of expenditure tax.

text.p: India's centre-left ruling coalition could widen the scope of a federal expenditure tax to cover luxury items like cars and high-end consumer durables in its annual budget, analysts said on Thursday.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram was scheduled to present the 1997/98 budget for the fiscal year beginning on April 1 to parliament at 5 p.m. (1130 GMT) on Friday.
"The government must raise tax revenues and they have to find a socially acceptable way of doing it," said Rupa Bose, strategist at Paribas Capital Markets in Singapore.
"A luxury or expenditure tax would be politically accepted and it wouldn't hurt market sentiment too much. People who buy these products, in most cases, won't stop buying them."
A federal expenditure tax of 10 percent is currently imposed on hotel tariffs which exceed 1,200 rupees ($35).
Bose said new targets could include cigarettes, high-end consumer durables, air travel, liquor and five-star hotels.
Analysts said automobiles could take the biggest hit.

"We expect the government to impose an expenditure tax on luxury commodities such as luxury diesel cars, particularly diesel since consumers get a subsidy on diesel," securities firm James Capel B&K said in a pre-budget report.
Some automobile analysts said the increase in taxes for diesel cars could come in the form of a 10 percentage point rise in excise duties to 50 percent.
They said the higher levies -- whether in the form of increased excise or an expenditure tax -- would hurt demand for diesel cars.
Economist Bidisha Ganguly at W.I. Carr Securities said it was unclear what form the tax would take.
"Tax revenues as a percentage of GDP have stagnated," Ganguly said, referring to gross domestic product. "You can't really raise tax rates any more because they are already very high."
She said tax revenues as a percentage of GDP had dropped slightly to 10.1 percent in 1995/96 from 10.9 percent in 1991/92. Fewer than two of every 100 Indian citizens pay taxes.

"The government has to widen the tax base. How do you capture all those people who are earning enough but not paying taxes?" Ganguly said, adding that one way out was to increase the scope of the expenditure tax.
Newspaper reports said levies could be imposed on Indians living abroad, telephone owners, heavy consumers of electricity and passengers on domestic air routes.
Some reports forecast an expenditure-based assessment on professionals like doctors and engineers.

"There's a kind of Robin Hood attitude. The government is saying that the people who can afford to pay should pay so that the less fortunate can live off their expense," said R. Balakrishan, president of securities firm Dil Vikas Finance Ltd.
